newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Italy struggles to rejoin EU money club.
newsitem.headline: Italy struggles to rejoin EU money club.

text.p: Italy's attempts to rejoin the European Union's currency club will be on the line on Sunday when finance ministers from the 15-nation bloc meet in emergency session to hammer out a rate for entry.

The EU's monetary committee of central bank and finance ministry officials failed on Saturday after almost nine hours of talks to let the lira back into the exchange rate mechanism (ERM) after a four-year absence.
Italy, officials said, was asking to come in at too weak a level, worrying its partners about the effect on their industries.
It was left to the finance ministers themselves to find a solution. If one is not found by the time financial markets open on Monday, market reaction could be ferocious.

Re-joining the ERM, from which the lira was unceremoniously dumped amid a currency crisis in 1992, is seem by Italy as crucial to its hopes for being in the first wave of EU countries to adopt a single currency in 1999.
A stable two-year stint within the ERM is one of the qualifying criteria for the new currency, the Euro.
The ERM is designed to allow member currencies to trade within bands against each other -- for the most part fluctuating by no more than 15 percent from a central rate.
Officials told Reuters that Italy had asked to rejoin at a central rate of 1,010 lira to the German mark, the key currency in the grid.
It was far too weak for the others' blood, however. They said they wanted a rate of less than 1,000 lira to the mark. The lira was trading at about 999 to the mark on Friday.
France has been the most vehement in wanting a stronger rate from the lira, having seen some of its industries battered by a neighbour with a weaker currency.

But Germany, too, is wary of Italy's attempts to be among the first in the single currency. The powerful Bundesbank is insistent that all currencies becoming part of the Euro be strong and be based on sustainable ecomomic policies.
EU countries which want to join are rushing to meet targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, budget deficits and public debt in 1997 -- necessary if they are to be at the start.
Seeking to trim their deficits to no more than three percent of Gross Domestic Product, however, some have unveiled controversial one-off budgetary measures to bring their deficits under control.
Italy has proposed a so-called Euro-tax, a one-off revenue raiser ro help it meet the targets.
If, as expected, Italy is brought into the ERM, only three of the EU's 15 countries will be outside the grid.
Britain and Sweden argue that it is not necessary to be in the ERM to qualify for the Euro, it is enough to have a stable rate with the other countries.
Both countries are sceptical about the Euro project.
Greece's economy is far weaker that the others and membership of the single currency is all-but ruled out.
